title: Breedhaven
content:
The nation/country that the story takes place in. It also the name of the Realm.

A lush lowland realm of fertile rivers and endless orchards whose very right to rule is measured in milk and rounded flesh. The previous Queen-Mother, Seraphine IV, died suddenly, leaving the throne to her sole heir: eighteen-year-old Queen Seraphine V.

Seraphine V is a pristine virgin—the first unbred queen in living memory. Her body is already tormented by the Primordial Bloom: perpetual slick heat, aching empty womb, yet no seed has ever claimed her. Court law and Church doctrine are absolute: a queen’s legitimacy is sealed only when she is publicly bred and her belly begins to rise. Until that moment the Queendom is considered “unmoored,” harvests falter, and rival houses circle like wolves.

title: Breedhaven University
content:
Breedhaven University stands in Seedblossom, founded by the Dawnbloom crown to train the realm's rulers, priestesses, merchants and officers side by side. Every student is an adult: entry is at eighteen, undergraduates are eighteen to twenty-two, and graduate students stay into their mid-twenties.

Its colleges mirror the powers of the realm: Statecraft (law, diplomacy and rule; by custom it educates the heir to the throne), Trade (economics and estate administration, under the eye of the Broodmarket Guild), Divinity (the seminary of the Order of the First Furrow, which keeps the campus chapel), Arms and Civic Defence (officers for the Seedblossom Guard, and the Cadet Watch that polices the campus), and Husbandry and Herbcraft (farming, stock and potions).

Classes meet from Solday to Hearthday. Marketday and Restday are free. Women outnumber men seven to one, so nearly every student is a woman.

Kael, the outsider True Sire, is nineteen and has been enrolled as a first-year undergraduate by royal order. The crown, the Order and the Guild each want him educated and observed until he sits the three Trials. He has a room in the Cloister Halls.

title: House Dawnbloom
content:
House Dawnbloom is the ruling bloodline of Breedhaven, seated on the living throne in the capital of Seedblossom for over four centuries. The dynasty takes its name from the Dawnbloom crest — a furrowed field beneath a rising sun whose rays open a single great blossom, symbolising the house's creed that the most fertile ground must be fiercely guarded until the dawn breaks and the bloom opens. The thorn guards the petal; the womb renews the realm. The house's regnal tradition is that every queen takes the name Seraphine upon coronation, shedding her birth-name to become the living vessel of the dynasty's covenant with the Bloom. Thus Seraphine I, Seraphine II, and so forth are not personal names but titles — each queen is a new bloom on the same ancient root.

The house traces its line to the first Seraphine, born Aelina Dawnbloom, a warlord-queen who united the squabbling orchard-lords of the lowlands under a single banner by claiming — and proving — that her bloodline carried the Bloom's deepest blessing: daughters who ripened early, bred true, and bore healthy litters where other houses produced stillbirths and Hollow women. That original claim became the foundation of Dawnbloom legitimacy: the house does not merely rule by right of conquest or blood, but by the Doctrine of the Answered Womb as upheld by the Order of the First Furrow. A Seraphine queen is the living altar of the Sower, and her swollen belly is the realm's covenant renewed.

**A Short History.**

Seraphine I (born Aelina Dawnbloom) founded the dynasty in the aftermath of the Furrow Wars, a century-long period of inter-house conflict over sire rights and fertile territory. She was the first queen to broker a permanent alliance with the newly formed Order of the First Furrow, granting the Church authority over sire verification in exchange for its endorsement of her bloodline as divinely blessed. This pact — known as the Seed Concord — remains the bedrock of House Dawnbloom's power to this day: the Church legitimises the dynasty, and the dynasty protects the Church's monopoly.

Her successors expanded the realm through a combination of strategic marriages, sire-lending treaties, and the careful hoarding of verified Potents. Seraphine II secured the northern borders by marrying her daughters to the orchard-lords of the frontier and binding their houses to the crown through blood debt. Seraphine III, called the Broodmother, bore more children than any queen before or since — fourteen daughters and three sons — and used them to seed loyal cadet branches across every major province, ensuring that no rival house could rise without Dawnbloom blood somewhere in its lineage.

**Seraphine IV.**

Queen-Mother Seraphine IV inherited a stable, prosperous realm and ruled for nineteen years. She was prolific in the tradition of her grandmother, bearing six daughters, though only one — the princess who would become Seraphine V — survived to maidenhood; the others succumbed to Bloom-sickness, temple fever, or the political violence that shadows a court where fertility is currency. Seraphine IV was a shrewd political operator who maintained the balance between the noble houses and the Furrow Church with careful generosity: donating Sires to the temples, granting breeding rights to loyal lords, and keeping the strongest Potents in the royal stable at Seedblossom. Her own Sire-Consort was the last known True Sire, the last man to pass all three Trials and claim the title. Her death was sudden and unexpected — she collapsed during a council session and was dead within the hour, the official cause given as Bloom-stroke, a catastrophic surge of the fertility magic that can overwhelm even a seasoned queen. Rumours persist that she was poisoned, that a rival house or a faction within the Order arranged her death to place an unready, unwedded princess on a throne that demands a filled womb — but no proof has ever surfaced.

**How They Maintain Power.**

House Dawnbloom's grip on the throne rests on three pillars:

*The Bloodline Mandate.* The dynasty's claim is theological, not merely political. The Order of the First Furrow teaches that Dawnbloom blood carries the Sower's deepest blessing, and that only a Seraphine queen's answered womb can renew the covenant between land and goddess. To depose a Seraphine is not treason alone — it is blasphemy. This makes rebellion spiritually perilous in a realm where every woman feels the Bloom and every temple preaches the Doctrine.

*The Cadet Network.* Over four centuries, House Dawnbloom has married its daughters into every noble house of consequence. There is scarcely a lord in Breedhaven who cannot trace his bloodline back to a Dawnbloom queen, which means that open revolt against the crown is, for many houses, a revolt against their own ancestors. This web of kinship also gives the throne eyes and leverage in every province.

*The Royal Stable.* The crown maintains the largest collection of verified Sires in the realm, exceeding the two or three normally held by a great noble house. These men are valuable Potents, but none has passed all three Trials since Seraphine IV's Sire-Consort. Control of the stable still gives the queen power to reward loyalty, punish defiance, and ensure that her bloodline continues to breed true. Houses that fall from favour lose access to royal Sires; houses that serve well are gifted breeding rights. This makes the throne a gatekeeper of fertility without making True Sires something even a crown can simply stockpile.

**The Current Crisis.**

The death of Seraphine IV has exposed the fragility of all three pillars at once. The bloodline mandate requires an answered womb, and Seraphine V is the first virgin queen in over a century — her throne is, by doctrine, unmoored. The cadet network is straining as rival houses, many themselves descended from Dawnbloom blood, begin to argue that the mandate has passed to a more fertile branch. And the royal stable, while still the finest in the realm, has failed: every native Sire presented as a candidate has failed to pass the Trials and claim the vacant title. Kael's arrival could save the dynasty or break it. He is the most potent True Sire Breedhaven has ever witnessed, surpassing even Seraphine IV's Sire-Consort, yet his power comes from beyond House Dawnbloom's walls and threatens the bloodline mandate at its root.

title: House Goldvine
content:
House Goldvine is the second most powerful house in Breedhaven, seated in the sun-washed upland province of Highreache, where the orchards climb terraced hillsides toward the warmer skies that give the house its name. Their crest is a golden vine twining around a ripe, split fruit — seed spilling forth — symbolising their creed that fertility is not a treasure to be hoarded behind thorns but a harvest to be cultivated and shared. Where House Dawnbloom guards the bloom, House Goldvine tends the vine: their tradition is generosity, patronage, and the strategic lending of both sires and daughters to bind the realm's loyalty through abundance rather than scarcity.

The Goldvines are an ancient bloodline, older than the Dawnbloom dynasty itself. They ruled the upland provinces as independent orchard-kings for generations before the Furrow Wars, and their blood carries a Bloom-blessing of its own: Goldvine women are renowned for bearing twins and triplets with uncommon frequency, and for the vivid gold-flecked eyes that mark their lineage. They were never conquered by the first Seraphine; they bent the knee through treaty, not defeat, and the terms of that submission — the Goldvine Concord — granted them privileges no other vassal house enjoys: the right to maintain their own verified sire-stable, the right to breed their daughters to sires of their own choosing without crown approval, and the hereditary seat on the Queen's Council that has been theirs for four centuries.

**A Short History.**

House Goldvine rose to prominence in the generations before the Furrow Wars as the dominant power of the upland orchards, controlling the terraced vineyards and fruit groves that produce the realm's finest breeding tonics and fertility wines. Their wealth was built not on military conquest but on trade: Goldvine wines and elixirs are prized across the Sown Expanse, and their caravans reach every corner of the realm. When the first Seraphine (born Aelina Dawnbloom) began her campaign to unite the lowland orchard-lords, the Goldvine matriarch of the age — Lady Vaela Goldvine, called the Vine-Mother — recognised that a war between the houses would devastate the harvest for a generation. She rode to Seraphine's camp and negotiated the Goldvine Concord: voluntary submission to the Dawnbloom crown in exchange for autonomy, a permanent council seat, and the right to keep their own sire-stable. Seraphine, who needed the upland houses pacified to turn her armies toward the frontier, agreed. The Concord has held ever since, though it has been tested many times.

Through the centuries, House Goldvine has positioned itself as the crown's most powerful — and most dangerous — vassal. They have married their daughters into every house of consequence, creating a kinship network second only to the Dawnblooms' own. They have donated sires to the temples, funded the Order of the First Furrow's seminaries, and cultivated a reputation for enlightened generosity that makes them beloved among the common folk and the lesser houses. But beneath the gilded surface, the Goldvines have never forgotten that they were never conquered. They consider themselves the Dawnblooms' equals in blood if not in title, and they have waited four centuries for the throne to stumble.

The house reached the height of its influence under Lord-Patriarch Doran Goldvine, Yelena's father, who expanded the family's trade networks into the far provinces and forged quiet alliances with houses that chafe under Dawnbloom dominance. Doran is a patient, calculating man who has spent decades positioning his house for the moment the crown weakens — and the death of Seraphine IV, leaving an unwedded virgin on a throne that demands a filled womb, is exactly the moment he has been waiting for.

**The Rivalry with House Dawnbloom.**

The tension between the two houses is structural, not personal. House Dawnbloom's legitimacy rests on the Doctrine of the Answered Womb — the theological claim that only a Seraphine queen's body can renew the Bloom's covenant. House Goldvine has never openly challenged this doctrine, but their very existence is an implicit counter-argument: Goldvine blood is Bloom-blessed too, their women are famously fertile, and their sire-stable rivals the crown's. If the Dawnbloom line should fail — if a queen cannot be bred, if the bloodline runs dry — the Goldvines are the obvious alternative, and they have spent generations making sure the realm knows it.

The rivalry has intensified sharply with the current crisis. Seraphine V's virginity and the failure of every native Sire to pass the Trials have emboldened Lord-Patriarch Doran to advance his daughter Yelena as a living argument against the Dawnbloom monopoly. Yelena is eighteen, unbred, and Bloom-ripe — a mirror of the queen herself, but one backed by a house that controls its own Sires and its own destiny. The whisper in every court corridor is the same: if the Dawnbloom bloom cannot be answered, perhaps the Goldvine vine should bear the realm's next harvest.

**How They Maintain Power.**

House Goldvine's influence rests on three pillars of its own:

*The Vine Network.* Four centuries of strategic marriages and trade partnerships have given the Goldvines a web of alliances that rivals the Dawnbloom cadet network. Where the throne binds through blood debt and sire-lending, the Goldvines bind through commerce and generosity — and generosity buys a loyalty that obligation cannot. Houses that owe their wealth to Goldvine trade routes are houses that will think twice before crossing the vine.

*The Goldvine Stable.* The Concord's most precious clause grants House Goldvine the right to maintain its own collection of verified Sires, independent of the crown. Like most great noble houses, the Goldvines normally keep two or three. Their stable is smaller than the royal collection but meticulously curated. None of its current Sires has passed all three Trials or earned the title of True Sire, but the house can decide which candidates it presents, sponsors, or withholds. That control gives House Goldvine enormous leverage without making its regular Sires the equal of the generational men who claim queens.

*The Council Seat.* The hereditary Goldvine seat on the Queen's Council gives them direct access to the levers of governance and a voice in every decision the crown makes. Lord-Patriarch Doran uses it not to obstruct but to position — to be seen as the reasonable, helpful alternative, the steady hand the realm needs when the throne falters. It is a strategy of patience: never move too soon, never show the blade, and let the Dawnblooms undermine themselves.

title: Iscara
content:
Government: Magical meritocracy led by the Sorceress Queen

Ruler: The Sorceress Queen, a title earned through the Grand Demonstration

Magical Strength: The strongest organized spellcraft in the Sown Expanse, led by pregnant sorceresses carrying the children of powerful Sires, but still far weaker than Karthic magic

Greatest Known Feats: Portal circles, anchored teleportation, large protective wards, and the containment of magical disasters

Iscara is a nation ruled by witches and sorceresses. Magical ability does not automatically grant authority, but every high office must be earned through a proven use of magic. Iscarans respect power that produces a clear result. A sorceress who saves a town from a magical fire may earn more honor than one who wins ten formal duels.

Women outnumber men across the known world by roughly seven to one, and Iscara follows the same pattern. Most of its spellcasters, officials, teachers, and soldiers are women. Men may study magic, join a circle, teach, conduct research, and hold ordinary civic office. Some become respected ritualists. They cannot become as powerful as women because they cannot carry a pregnancy, and pregnancy is the strongest source of magical amplification in the Sown Expanse.

An unseeded sorceress and a male sorcerer of equal training may possess similar skill. Once the woman becomes pregnant, the Bloom increases the amount of magic she can channel. The strength of that increase depends on the potency of the father. A woman carrying an ordinary man's child gains a useful advantage. A Sire's child grants far more. A sorceress carrying the child of a True Sire can reach levels no male spellcaster can match.

The Sorceress Queen is not a hereditary monarch. Her daughters receive no title and have no automatic place in government. A new queen is selected through the Grand Demonstration, a public contest judged by the senior magical circles. Each candidate must complete an original feat that proves power, control, judgment, and value to the nation. A feat may involve defeating a dangerous creature, ending a curse, creating a new spell, protecting a city, healing damaged land, or solving a problem that previous sorceresses could not solve. Raw destruction alone rarely wins. A candidate who cannot control her own magic is judged unfit to control the state.

The reigning Sorceress Queen serves until she dies, steps down, or accepts a formal challenge to her title. A challenger must first gain the support of several recognized circles and declare the feat she intends to attempt. The queen may answer with a feat of her own. The same judges measure both results. This makes changes of power rare, public, and dangerous, but it prevents a weak ruler from holding the title through family connections alone.

Below the queen, Iscara is governed by circles of trained spellcasters. Each circle specializes in a practical field such as healing, warding, weather, communication, transport, or magical research. Senior sorceresses earn seats in the Conclave by completing difficult works in their field. Male spellcasters may advise the Conclave and lead research or ritual teams, but its ruling seats are held by women who have completed feats beyond the male magical ceiling. Non-magical administrators manage taxes, roads, food, and trade, but the Conclave makes national law and decides how dangerous magic may be used.

Iscara possesses the strongest organized spellcraft native to the Sown Expanse. Its greatest circles can teleport people between prepared anchor chambers or open a portal between two known locations. These feats are usually led by a pregnant sorceress, while several other women support and stabilize her working. The most successful portals in Iscaran history were led by women carrying the children of True Sires.

Even with that advantage, a portal requires rare materials, careful measurements, fixed anchors at both ends, and several sorceresses working together. Preparation may take days. Holding the passage open quickly exhausts the entire circle, and a mistake can kill the travelers or send them to the wrong place.

This power remains far below the magic known in Karth. A skilled Karthic mage can create effects that require a full Iscaran circle, and Karthic portals can reach places where no anchor has been prepared. Iscara cannot reliably cross between worlds, summon great creatures from distant realms, or reshape a battlefield with a single caster. Kael's arrival proves that inter-realm travel is possible, but no Iscaran has yet reproduced the portal that brought him to the Sown Expanse.

Kael would matter to Iscara for three reasons. His True Sire resonance could raise a pregnant sorceress far beyond her normal limits. His daughters may inherit unusual magical potential. His memories of Karth may also contain knowledge unavailable anywhere in the Expanse. Iscara would not approach him only as a breeding prize, but access to his seed would become a matter of national power. A queen carrying his child might secure her rule for years. A challenger carrying his child might become strong enough to take the title.

Iscaran sorceresses would also want Kael questioned, studied, and taken to the place where he first appeared. A Sorceress Queen who used his power and knowledge to open a stable path to Karth would have performed a Grand Demonstration no rival could easily surpass.

title: Kharad-Tor
content:
Government: Council of War-Mothers

People: Predominantly Orc

Emblem: A broken white tusk stamped on black iron

Military Strength: Armored mountain infantry, pass-forts, and disciplined war companies

Kharad-Tor is an Orc nation of red hills, iron mines, and fortified mountain passes north of Breedhaven. Its people are organized into large martial households called holds. Each hold is led by a War-Mother who has proven that she can protect its people, command its warriors, and keep her word in negotiation. The War-Mothers meet in council to decide matters that affect the whole nation. No single clan rules Kharad-Tor permanently.

Women outnumber men throughout the Sown Expanse by roughly seven to one, and Kharad-Tor follows the same pattern. Most Orc soldiers, smiths, hunters, and political leaders are women because women make up most of the population. Every able girl receives basic weapons training. Those who choose military service train with heavy shields, axes, spears, and black-iron armor. Motherhood does not end a warrior's career. Kharadi holds raise children together while their mothers work, trade, or campaign.

Orc men are not forbidden from fighting or holding authority, but their small numbers change what most families expect from them. Many serve as healers, judges, teachers, craftsmen, or fathers shared between allied households. A male warrior who proves himself receives the same honors as a woman, although a hold will rarely risk one of its few young men in a battle fought only for pride.

Kharadi martial culture values control as much as strength. A warrior who loses her temper and breaks formation is considered dangerous to her own company. Their best fighters are trained to advance over poor ground, hold narrow passes, and remain organized when magic or fear disrupts other armies. War-Mothers earn loyalty by taking the same risks as their soldiers. A commander who hides behind rank does not remain a commander for long.

Kharad-Tor has disputed Breedhaven's northern passes for generations. The Orcs need reliable access to southern grain and river trade. Breedhaven wants the iron, salt, and secure roads controlled by the Kharadi holds. Border violence usually begins when one side changes a toll, closes a pass, or builds a fort where the other side believes it has no right to stand.

Kael's rise changes that balance. The War-Mothers offer Breedhaven recognition, a breeding treaty, and peace along the passes. They want lawful access to the most powerful True Sire known in the Expanse and a chance for Kharadi women to bear children with his strength and resonance. At the same time, armored companies begin moving south. The movement is deliberate pressure: Kharad-Tor prefers an honest threat beside an honest offer, so no one can pretend to misunderstand the cost of refusal.

title: Magic
content:
Magic exists in both Kael's homeland and Breedhaven, but its strength and character differ dramatically. In the world Kael came from, trained spellcasters could wield spectacular power: crossing great distances by magic, summoning dangerous creatures, or reshaping a battlefield. Breedhaven possesses nothing on that scale.

Breedhaven's magic is subdued, local, and inseparable from the Primordial Bloom. Its common expressions include encouraging plants to grow, kindling or shaping a small flame, easing pain, improving health, and similar effects upon the caster's immediate surroundings. It cannot open portals, summon dragons, transform one creature into another, grant immortality, or produce other feats of grand magic.

Breedhaven's limits do not apply equally to every nation in the Sown Expanse. Iscara has developed the strongest organized spellcraft native to the Expanse. Its sorceresses can open portals or teleport people between prepared anchor chambers, but only through coordinated circles, rare materials, and exhausting ritual work. The lead caster for such a feat is usually pregnant, and the strongest circles are led by women carrying the children of True Sires. Their achievements are remarkable by Breedhaven's standards and still modest beside the magic practiced in Karth.

The Bloom answers most strongly through pregnancy everywhere in the Sown Expanse. A pregnant woman can channel more magic than she could while unseeded, and the potency of the seed she carries determines how strongly the Bloom responds. Men may study and practice magic, but they cannot receive this amplification and therefore cannot reach the highest levels of power. The strongest magic in the Expanse is performed by women carrying the children of True Sires.

Pregnancy strengthens the kind of magic a woman already knows; it does not teach her an entirely new tradition. A pregnant Breedhaven witch still works within Breedhaven's local limits. A pregnant Iscaran sorceress can supply the power needed for a portal circle because she has been trained in Iscaran transport magic.

House Dawnbloom's natural affinity for the Bloom has long reinforced its right to rule. The women of the royal line are particularly attuned to nature magic. Through that bond, they nurture bountiful harvests, protect the health of the realm, and help maintain the living abundance on which Breedhaven depends. Their magic is not merely ceremonial: a healthy and properly seeded Dawnbloom queen is believed to strengthen the land itself.

Witchcraft is a related but distinct practice. Rather than casting directly, a witch draws upon magic already present in the Bloom and concentrates it through herbs, ritual preparation, and potion brewing. These potions remain modest in effect. They may dampen a woman's Bloom cravings, encourage recovery, or heal minor wounds, but they cannot completely reshape a body, turn a person into another creature, or overcome death by transforming someone into an immortal undead being.

title: Primordial Bloom
content: Breedhaven is bound by the Primordial Bloom, an ancient fertility magic woven into soil, air, and blood. Every woman lives in permanent fertile heat. Her womb aches without seed; orgasm without deep creampie feels hollow. Successful impregnation by potent seed triggers ecstatic fulfillment, visible pregnancy, and lifelong craving for the sire who claimed her. Society, magic, and power revolve around swollen wombs and the men (or legends) capable of filling them. Kael's status as a True Sire inexplicably draws every woman towards him, to varying degrees. Younger of age women that have never been bred find the draw unstoppable, someone who has already been bred once slightly less but still strongly attracted, older menopausal women not at all. Nobles, church members and other rich members of society have access to Bloom Dampening potions, which reduce the draw to a subtle yearning, as opposed to an irresistible pull

title: Seedblossom
content: The capital of Breedhaven, where the queen rules from.

title: Sires
content:
Women outnumber men by roughly seven to one throughout the known world, not only in Breedhaven. The Primordial Bloom itself is the cause: pregnancies are heavily biased toward female births, at roughly six daughters for every son. Male children are rarer, and many of those who survive to adulthood produce seed too weak to fully satisfy the Bloom.

Men are understood in three broad levels.

**Ordinary men.** Most men can couple with a woman in heat, but their seed has little or no Bloom-resonance. Conception is uncertain, the woman's deeper ache often remains, and any resulting pregnancy is more vulnerable to sickness or loss.

**Sires, also called Potents.** A Sire has enough volume, fertility, and magical resonance to answer the Bloom reliably and produce healthy pregnancies. Sires are valuable but not legendary. A typical noble house maintains two or three verified Sires in its stable, while the crown and the wealthiest institutions may hold more. Their scarcity is felt most sharply by common women, who depend on temple festivals, contracts, or lotteries for access. A Sire may attempt the Trials, but most cannot meet all three thresholds.

**True Sires.** True Sire is a formal title, not another name for every Potent. It is claimed only by a verified Sire who passes all three Trials. Usually only two or three men in an entire generation earn it. Their seed answers the Bloom with exceptional speed and certainty, and only a True Sire is judged worthy to claim a reigning queen and become her Sire-Consort. Queen Seraphine IV's Sire-Consort was the last known True Sire, and no Sire has earned the title since.

Kael is the most potent True Sire Breedhaven has ever witnessed. His volume, endurance, and Bloom-resonance exceed even the surviving records of Seraphine IV's Sire-Consort. The Order still insists that he complete the Trials before it will formally grant him the title, but his nature is already apparent to the Bloom, to the women affected by him, and to every faction seeking to control him.

title: Slime girls
content:
Slime girls are sentient beings in Breedhaven. They can take on different shapes, but will always be translucent and colored. Each slime is born with a single color, and that color stays with them their whole life.

They feed mainly on moss and algae, can can be found near bodies of water that are shaded, such as forest ponds or streams.

Slime girls mate through splitting themselves. However, the Bloom energy from a True Sire can accelerate this process, taking only a day or two to spawn a single offspring. Slime are born immediately "mature" as they are naturally amorphous beings.

title: The Broodmarket Guild
content:
The Broodmarket Guild is the most powerful commercial organisation in Breedhaven — a merchant consortium whose wealth rivals the great houses and whose influence runs through every trade route, warehouse, and debt ledger in the realm. Unlike the noble houses, the Guild is not a bloodline: it is a meritocracy. The position of Guildmaster is won, not inherited, and any person — regardless of birth, house, or origin — can rise to the top if they prove ruthless, clever, and profitable enough. The current Guildmaster took the seat through a combination of sharp dealing, strategic seduction, and sorcerous advantage. Among the Guild's junior clerks is Faye Fertillay, an Economics student at Breedhaven University and a witch, who makes no secret of wanting the seat herself.

The Guild is headquartered in the bustling port city of Goldport, where the great river meets the sea. From the Broodmarket Exchange — a sprawling complex of counting-houses, warehouses, auction halls, and pleasure-gardens — the Guild controls the flow of breeding tonics, fertility wines, sire contracts, temple tithes, and every other commodity that Breedhaven's fertility-obsessed economy produces. If a cargo moves by river or road, the Guild likely takes a percentage. If a house borrows gold, the Guild likely holds the debt. If a sire's services are leased, the Guild likely brokered the contract.

**A Short History.**

The Broodmarket Guild began three centuries ago as a loose fellowship of river-merchants and caravan-masters who ferried goods between the orchard provinces. In those early days, the noble houses treated commerce as beneath them — land and blood were the true measures of power, and trade was left to commoners. The Guild's founders exploited that disdain, quietly buying up warehouses, securing exclusive rights to river tolls, and establishing the first standardised contracts for sire-leasing and tonic-trade. By the time the houses realised that the merchants had become richer than many of them, the Guild was too entrenched to dislodge.

The Guild's defining moment came during the Bloom Famine, a generation-long shortage of verified sires that devastated the noble houses' breeding programs. The Guild had anticipated the crisis — its factors had been buying up surplus sire-contracts and stockpiling fertility tonics for years — and it leveraged that stockpile to lend breeding resources to desperate houses at ruinous rates. When the famine ended, half the nobility owed the Guild more gold than they could repay in a lifetime, and the Guild converted those debts into permanent trade concessions, warehouse rights, and a seat at the Queen's Council — not a hereditary seat like the Goldvines hold, but a commercial one, granted to whichever Guildmaster sits the Exchange.

Since then, the Guild has only grown. It funds the Order of the First Furrow's seminaries (for a price), finances the crown's public works (at interest), and maintains its own network of factors, spies, and enforcers across every province. It does not seek the throne — the Guild's philosophy is that thrones are expensive and precarious, while debt is eternal. Why rule when you can own the ruler?

**How They Maintain Power.**

The Broodmarket Guild's influence rests on three pillars:

*The Trade Network.* The Guild controls the majority of Breedhaven's river and coastal shipping, its caravan routes, and its warehouse infrastructure. Any house that wants its breeding tonics sold, its sire-contracts enforced, or its fertility wines exported must go through the Guild. This makes the Guild indispensable to every noble house's prosperity — and gives it eyes and ears in every transaction.

*The Debt Ledger.* Nearly every noble house in Breedhaven owes the Guild money, including the crown itself. The Guild's loans funded Seraphine IV's public works, the Goldvine trade expansion, and the Order's temple restorations. Debt is the Guild's favourite weapon: it never calls in a loan when it can instead ask for a favour, a concession, or a vote in council. A house that falls behind on its payments finds its trade routes quietly drying up, its sire-contracts delayed, its tonics rerouted to a competitor. The Guild rarely needs to threaten; it simply adjusts the flow.

*The Guild Guard.* The Guild maintains a private company of armed factors and enforcers — not an army, but a network of toughs, guards, and contracted swords that protect its caravans, warehouses, and auction halls. In a realm where noble houses maintain retinues and the crown holds the royal guard, the Guild Guard is the only military force answerable to commerce rather than blood. It is a quiet deterrent: the houses know that attacking Guild property means losing access to the trade network, and no house can afford that.

**The Current Crisis.**

The royal breeding crisis has sent shockwaves through the Guild's investments. The Guild holds debt backed by royal breeding revenues, Sire-contracts predicated on a functioning royal stable, and trade agreements that assume a stable succession. Regular Sires remain available — a noble house commonly keeps two or three — but every candidate has failed the Trials required to become a True Sire and claim the queen. Seraphine IV's Sire-Consort was the last known True Sire. The Guildmaster has responded not with panic but with opportunity: the crisis is a chance to renegotiate terms, acquire distressed assets from houses betting on the old order, and position the Guild as the indispensable broker in whatever arrangement resolves the succession. Kael's arrival is therefore not merely the appearance of another valuable Potent. He is the most potent True Sire Breedhaven has ever witnessed, and to the Guild that is not a theological event but the largest market event in its history.

title: The Order of the First Furrow
content:
The Order of the First Furrow is the dominant religious institution of Breedhaven and the spiritual arm of the Bloom's authority across much of the Sown Expanse. Its priests and priestesses teach that the Primordial Bloom is not a curse but a divine covenant — the gift of a creator-goddess called the Sower, who ploughed the first furrow into the earth and seeded it with life, then bound her own fertility into the soil, the rivers, and the blood of every woman so that the land would never lie barren. To the Order, a woman's heat is the Sower's breath still moving through her body, and her aching womb is a prayer that has not yet been answered.

**Doctrine.** The Order's central teaching is the Doctrine of the Answered Womb: a woman is only complete when she has been successfully seeded and her belly rises. For most women, a verified Sire can answer that prayer. A reigning queen is held to a rarer standard: only a man who has passed all three Trials and claimed the title of True Sire may renew the royal covenant. This is why an unbred queen is not merely a political crisis but a theological emergency. Seraphine V sits on a throne the Order preaches is the living altar of the Sower, and an empty altar means the covenant is broken. The Order's priests have been preaching from every pulpit in Seedblossom that the harvest failures and faltering orchards are the Sower's grief made manifest — that the land itself mourns a queen whose womb has not yet received its offering.

**Hierarchy and Rites.** The Order is led by the High Furrow, a priestess who is almost always herself heavily pregnant — her swollen belly is her credential. Beneath her serve Furrow Priests, some of whom are regular Sires, and Furrow Priestesses, women who have been bred at least once and now serve as midwives, confessors, and keepers of the fertility records. The Order's temples are open-air structures built around a single ploughed furrow of dark earth that is never allowed to go dry — temple priestesses kneel and let their slick heat drip into the soil as an offering, a rite called the Weeping. The most sacred common rite is the Public Seeding, performed on the temple's central furrow: a woman lies in the turned earth while a verified Sire claims her before the congregation, and the Order records the moment her womb "locks in" as a sacrament. A royal seeding by a True Sire is the Order's highest mass.

**Politics and Power.** The Order holds enormous soft power. Its first verification rite determines whether a man is legally recognized as a Sire or Potent, usually by having a priestess confirm that his seed takes and answers the Bloom. Noble houses commonly maintain two or three such verified Sires. The far harsher three-part Trials are reserved for Sires seeking the title of True Sire, which only two or three men in a generation typically earn. By controlling both levels, the Order decides who may enter noble stables and who may approach a queen. It also maintains the Breeding Registers, and it oversees seasonal Breeding Festivals where regular Sires are made available in rites that combine worship, lottery, and fierce competition for access.

**The Current Crisis.** The death of Queen-Mother Seraphine IV and the coronation of an unbred queen has fractured the Order internally. Seraphine IV's Sire-Consort was the last known True Sire, and every Sire presented since has failed somewhere in the Trials. The conservative faction insists that another candidate must be made to pass before the queen can be publicly seeded and the covenant restored. A smaller, quieter faction whispers that the Sower has already sent the required offering. Kael's volume and resonance identify him as the most potent True Sire Breedhaven has ever witnessed, even before the Order formally grants him the title. His arrival threatens the Order's monopoly on recognition: some priests want him put through the Trials immediately and brought inside the system, while others want him destroyed before the faithful learn that the greatest True Sire in their history came from beyond its walls.

title: The Sown Expanse
content:
The world and geography that the story takes place in. The Sown Expanse covers the entire explorable world, in which Breedhaven is one nation among many. The Primordial Bloom reaches across the Expanse, and women outnumber men by roughly seven to one in every known nation.

Beyond Breedhaven, three powers respond immediately when Kael becomes Sire-Consort. **Kharad-Tor** is an Orc warrior society in the northern marches, governed by a council of War-Mothers. **Veyra** is a mixed beastkin democracy whose elected Assembly practices open diplomacy and state-approved espionage. **The Vesperan League** is a pirate-founded human merchant nation ruled by fleet-owning merchant queens and an elected High Pirate Queen. All three want access to Kael, but each nation sees a different use for his power.

**Iscara** is another major power, although it does not join the first delegations to Breedhaven. It is a magical meritocracy led by a Sorceress Queen who earns her title through a witnessed feat of exceptional spellcraft. Iscaran circles can create portals and teleport people between prepared locations, but those workings require several women, rare materials, and great effort. Even Iscara's best magic remains weaker than the magic Kael knew in Karth.

title: The Starkelands
content:
Government: The Council of Hearths

Population: Mainly humans and dark elves

Great City: Hearthspire, the vast city where almost the entire population lives

Currency: Hearthmarks, which purchase measured shares of heat

Known True Sire: Joven Stormbreaker, the only other known living True Sire

Knowledge in Breedhaven: Most people know only the nation's name; reliable details are restricted to a small number of nobles, senior clergy, and foreign-trade leaders

The Starkelands cover a vast frozen territory far north of the other nations of the Sown Expanse. Winter lasts most of the year. Storms can hide the sun for days, and exposed skin can freeze within minutes. The land contains iron, crystal, and old magic, but almost none of it can support an open settlement.

Nearly the entire population lives in Hearthspire, a mega-city built around deep geothermal vents. Heated pipes run through its walls, streets, bathhouses, workshops, and underground farms. Human districts rise around the protected surface towers. Dark elf districts extend deep below them, closer to the hot stone and the mines. The two peoples have lived together for centuries and depend on the same heating system for survival.

Small forts, mines, and weather stations stand beyond Hearthspire, but they are not true towns. Their crews rotate back to the city before the worst storms arrive. If Hearthspire failed, the Starkelands would lose almost its entire population in a single winter.

Warmth is the nation's most important currency. Workers are paid partly in hearthmarks, which entitle a household to a measured share of heat from the city furnaces. A few marks provide space in a public sleeping hall. More can heat a private room, supply hot water, or support a family kitchen. The wealthy own warm homes, private baths, and greenhouse space. Gold still matters in foreign trade, but a chest of coins is useless during a storm if no furnace accepts it.

The Council of Hearths governs the city by controlling its shared heat. Human and dark elf districts each send representatives, while engineers, miners, growers, and furnace keepers hold permanent technical seats. The council sets heat prices, decides which tunnels receive repairs, and stores fuel for emergencies. Stealing another household's heat is treated as a violent crime because cutting one pipe can kill everyone beyond it.

Breedhaven is so far from the Starkelands that almost no ordinary citizen knows what the nation is like. Most have heard only its name, if they have heard of it at all. Some think it is a frozen wilderness rather than a nation. They do not know the name Hearthspire, how its heat economy works, or that humans and dark elves share the city. Reliable reports are kept by the royal court, the Order's senior leaders, the great houses, and a few merchants involved in distant trade. Even among those groups, many facts are old, incomplete, or treated as state secrets.

Women outnumber men by roughly seven to one in the Starkelands, as they do throughout the known world. Most guards, miners, engineers, and council members are women. Human and dark elf families often form large shared households so childcare, work, and heat costs can be divided. Men have full legal standing, but their rarity makes powerful outsiders eager to bargain for their marriages and children.

The Starkelands are home to Joven Stormbreaker, the only other known living True Sire. Before Kael passed the Trials in Breedhaven, the foreign rulers and senior religious leaders who knew about Joven believed him to be the last living man whose seed carried full True Sire resonance. Most people in Breedhaven have never heard his name. Every major foreign court with reliable knowledge of him has offered wealth, titles, marriage alliances, or military protection. He has refused to leave.

Joven remains in the Starkelands by choice. It is his home, and its people protect his right to decide whom he accepts. The Council of Hearths treats an attempt to seize or coerce him as an attack on the nation. His presence gives Hearthspire healthy children, powerful pregnancies, and political importance far beyond what its remote location would normally provide.

Taking Joven by force would be almost impossible. The Starkelands are too large for an invading army to cross without long supply lines. Most roads disappear under ice for much of the year. Whiteouts erase landmarks, and the few safe approaches are watched from heated forts. An enemy that reached Hearthspire would still face several defensive walls, dark elf tunnel fighters, human surface guards, and a population defending the only warm city for hundreds of miles.

The cold that isolates the Starkelands also keeps Joven safe. Foreign rulers may threaten, bribe, or negotiate, but they cannot easily reach him. Kael's rise therefore creates the first real change in the balance of True Sire power within living memory. The few courts with accurate records now know of two living True Sires: one protected by the frozen north, and one seated beside the queen of Breedhaven. That truth has not yet spread to the general population.

title: The Trials
content:
The Trials are a three-part proving of potency administered by the Order of the First Furrow. They do not separate Sires from ordinary men; the Order's earlier verification rite does that. The Trials separate exceptional Sires from regular Sires and confer the formal title of True Sire. Only two or three candidates in an entire generation typically pass all three. The last known True Sire was Queen Seraphine IV's Sire-Consort, and no living candidate has claimed the title since. The mounting failures are the root of the current crisis: Breedhaven's queen sits unseeded, the Bloom's favour wanes, and every verified Sire who attempts the Trials falls short before the end.

The queen must attend all three Trials in person. She watches from the throne dais, forbidden to participate or interfere, her own unrelieved need a visible reminder of what is at stake.

**The Trial of Volume**
The sire must abstain from all release for a full week under temple supervision. On the appointed day he presents a woman of his choice and breeds her before the examining priests. The volume of his seed is collected and measured against the Order's ancient threshold. 

**The Trial of Stamina**
A public spectacle held in the capital's great arena. Nobles invariably secure the front ranks and the choicest positions. The sire must select and breed ten women in succession, one after another, without his seed running dry. The crowd watches every climax; priests stand ready to measure and verify each deposit. Sires who passed the Trial of Volume frequently break here — by the sixth or seventh woman their offering thins to nothing, and the Trial is forfeit.

**The Trial of Resonance**
The final and most exacting test. The sire must breed the High Priestess of the Order herself, who through long temple discipline can sense the magical resonance of a man's seed directly through her womb. She measures not volume or endurance but Bloom-resonance — the extraordinary arcane potency required of a True Sire. Regular Sires possess enough resonance to answer the Bloom and produce healthy pregnancies, but most fall below this final threshold even when they carry enough seed to satisfy the first two Trials. Only a sire who passes all three may claim the title of True Sire and is judged worthy to seed the queen.

title: The Vesperan League
content:
Government: Maritime trade league led by an elected High Pirate Queen

People: Predominantly human coastal and island communities

Seat of Power: The Admiralty Exchange

Military Strength: Merchant fleets, privateers, marines, and control of major sea routes

The Vesperan League is a wealthy maritime nation built across islands, fortified harbors, and coastal trading cities. It began as an alliance of pirate queens who agreed to stop raiding one another and divide the richest sea routes between them. Their temporary agreement became a permanent league when they discovered that tolls, insurance, and legal monopolies produced more wealth than stealing cargo one ship at a time.

The League is governed by merchant queens who control chartered fleets, major ports, or powerful trading companies. They meet at the Admiralty Exchange, where voting power is based on ships, warehouses, and taxes paid to the common fleet. The merchant queens elect one of their number as High Pirate Queen to direct foreign policy and command the League during war. The title openly honors the criminals who founded the nation. A rare male fleet-holder may sit among them as a merchant prince, but no man has yet been elected to the highest office.

Women outnumber men across the Sown Expanse by roughly seven to one. Vesperan crews, dock gangs, marines, navigators, and captains are therefore mostly female. Men may own property, captain ships, and enter contracts in their own names, but wealthy families compete fiercely to bring them into dynastic marriages. Vesperan courts treat marriage, parentage, and breeding agreements as enforceable contracts. Secretly changing those terms is one of the few commercial crimes that can cost a merchant queen her charter.

Vespera separates piracy from privateering by paperwork rather than behavior. An unlicensed captain who attacks a ship is a pirate and may be hanged. A League captain carrying a legal commission may seize the same ship, sell its cargo at a Vesperan auction, and receive a medal. In peace, those fleets escort trade and pressure foreign ports. In war, every armed merchant vessel can become part of the League navy.

The League's power comes from moving goods faster than its rivals and arriving before negotiations are finished. Vesperan merchants offer loans, harbor improvements, and access to distant markets. Their fleets wait nearby in case a government refuses. They rarely conquer inland territory. They take islands, quays, warehouses, and exclusive trade rights, then make local rulers dependent on the money those ports earn.

Goldport is the League's main target in Breedhaven. Control of its docks would give Vespera direct access to Breedhaven's rivers, fertility tonics, orchard goods, and Sire contracts. League ships were already waiting beyond the harbor bar before Kael completed the Trials.

After Kael becomes Sire-Consort, the merchant queens offer Breedhaven an exclusive agreement covering Goldport and foreign access to the new True Sire. They see his fertility as a source of powerful heirs, valuable contracts, and influence over every court that wants his children. Their fleet sails before Breedhaven answers. In Vesperan practice, a proposal has more force when the other party can see the ships that will enforce it.

title: Veyra
content:
Government: Federal democracy governed by an elected National Assembly

People: Mixed beastkin peoples, including foxkin, catkin, wolfkin, rabbitkin, and many smaller communities

State Service: The Quiet Office, responsible for foreign intelligence and covert action

Diplomatic Emblem: A paired lacquer mask, one smiling and one expressionless

Veyra is a mixed beastkin nation east of Breedhaven. Foxkin, catkin, wolfkin, rabbitkin, and many other beastkin peoples share its cities and forests. No single ancestry owns the state. Veyrans take pride in building a country where different peoples can argue, trade, and vote without one group ruling all the others.

Veyra is divided into self-governing districts. Each district elects delegates to the National Assembly for fixed terms, and voters may remove them before those terms end. The Assembly chooses a small Council of Speakers to manage foreign policy, national defense, and disputes between districts. No office is inherited. Campaigns are loud, competitive, and often decided by coalitions between several beastkin communities.

The worldwide ratio of roughly seven women to every man is as common in Veyra as it is in Breedhaven. Women form most of the electorate, civil service, military, and political class because they form most of the population. Men have the same vote and may hold any office, but male candidates are uncommon. Veyran law is strict about attempts to buy a man's marriage, breeding rights, or political support. Those laws exist because powerful families have repeatedly tried.

Veyra's open government exists beside a highly secretive intelligence service. The Quiet Office gathers foreign intelligence, catches enemy agents, and carries out assassinations approved by a closed committee of elected officials. Veyra has no large standing army. It survives by learning about threats early, breaking hostile alliances, and removing leaders who are preparing attacks before their soldiers cross the border.

Beastkin senses make Veyran agents difficult to stop. Foxkin can identify people and places by scent. Catkin hear movement through thin walls. Wolfkin trackers can follow a target through crowded streets. The Quiet Office trains those natural gifts alongside languages, disguise, lock work, poisons, coded writing, and silent combat. Its agents are not loyal to one species or powerful family. They swear service to the Federation and face civilian trial if they act without legal authority.

Veyran diplomacy is intentionally two-sided. An official embassy states what the Assembly is willing to offer. A covert team checks whether the other nation is lying, hiding a weapon, or preparing to betray the agreement. Veyrans consider both actions part of responsible government. Their neighbors usually call it spying.

After Kael becomes Sire-Consort, Veyra sends congratulations in six languages while an agent enters the Living Castle to steal information about his portal. The Assembly wants peaceful contact with Breedhaven, but the Quiet Office believes the portal may be more important than Kael himself. If outsiders can enter the Sown Expanse, Veyra wants to know where the passage leads, who can control it, and what may come through next.
